I haven't noticed any changes in my mood or interest, though, as I still feel sharp and really enjoy my DIY workshops and card games when I'm engaged—the struggle is just staying organized and on track.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me at what age you first noticed these symptoms of inattention and restlessness, and have they been present throughout your life or did they start more recently, perhaps around the time of your retirement?\n\nPatient: While these issues have become much more of a problem over the past year since I retired, they actually go all the way back to my childhood. It's something I've lived with my whole life, but it has just gotten much harder to manage lately with more commitments.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience significant hyperactivity, such as running, climbing, or being constantly on the go, during your childhood, or was it more about inattention and restlessness?\n\nPatient: As a child, it was definitely more about daydreaming and inattention rather than physical hyperactivity like running or climbing. In primary school, my teachers often told my parents that I was missing instructions and forgetting my books, though I could answer their questions just fine once they actually got my attention.\n\nDoctor: Now that you're an adult, do you find yourself often feeling the need to be on the go, or do you exhibit other signs of physical hyperactivity, such as tapping hands or feet, or leaving your seat in situations where you're expected to remain seated?\n\nPatient: While I don't run around wildly, I do experience a strong sense of internal restlessness and physical fidgetiness. During long meetings or in waiting rooms, I feel a constant urge to shift in my seat and look for excuses to stand up or walk to the hallway. Even when trying to sit quietly, my legs get so fidgety that I usually have to get up and tinker with something.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told or noticed that you have difficulty engaging in leisure activities quietly, such as reading or doing puzzles, due to feeling restless or a need to be active?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely have that difficulty. I like the idea of sitting and reading or doing quiet meditation at the senior center, but after just a few minutes my legs get fidgety and my mind starts wandering. I usually end up turning on the radio or getting up to tinker with something instead.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations, either currently or in the past, where you exhibited more overt signs of hyperactivity, such as excessive running, climbing, or an inability to engage in activities quietly, which might have been more pronounced than just feeling restless or fidgety?\n\nPatient: No, I don't recall ever having those kinds of overt physical behaviors like running around or climbing excessively, even when I was younger. For me, it has always been more about an internal sense of restlessness and having fidgety legs. I just find it very hard to sit through quiet activities without needing to shift around, stand up, or find something to tinker with.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that these symptoms have been present since childhood but have become more challenging to manage since your retirement. Can you tell me how these symptoms have specifically impacted your daily functioning and relationships, and have you noticed any periods where your symptoms improved or worsened significantly?\n\nPatient: Lately, these issues have caused me to double-book myself, miss appointments, and let down my family and the senior center, which has made my wife and kids lose trust in me and stop asking for my help. They became significantly worse and really stood out over the past year, right after I retired and tried to take on more responsibilities.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods in your life where you felt completely free of these symptoms of inattention, restlessness, and difficulty with quiet activities, or have they been consistently present, albeit with varying degrees of severity?\n\nPatient: No, I've never really been completely free of them; they have been pretty consistent throughout my life. Even back in primary school, I was always daydreaming and forgetting my books, but I managed to get by. It's only since retiring and taking on so many loose commitments without a fixed routine that these issues have really spiraled into a major problem.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant differences in how your symptoms affect you in structured versus unstructured environments, such as at work versus during retirement?\n\nPatient: Yes, shifting away from a fixed routine after retirement has made my symptoms much more noticeable. I now loosely structure my days around social and volunteer activities rather than a set schedule, and taking on more of these unstructured commitments over the past year has left me feeling overwhelmed, getting sidetracked, and missing appointments.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood but have worsened since retirement. Can you clarify if you experienced any significant improvement in your symptoms during your adult life, particularly during periods of high structure, such as when you were working, before they worsened again after retirement?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't thought about it deeply, but I think I always had some struggles. It’s this sudden lack of structure that made my family start worrying about my memory, whereas before I was able to handle it.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling restless and fidgety, but can you tell me if you've ever exhibited any signs of hyperactivity that interfered with your social, occupational, or other areas of functioning, such as excessive talking, feeling constantly on the go, or an inability to engage in activities quietly, and if so, how this has impacted your daily life?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't say I'm hyperactive in a loud way, but I definitely struggle to stay still and quiet, constantly shifting during long meetings or failing to sit through meditation because my legs get so fidgety.
